source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-11-03) Insight
finding: Describes the four-stage model (preparation, incubation, insight/illumination, verification), credited to Hadamard (1945, 1954 reprint). Gestalt school: seeing the problem in a new way, releasing past experience that blocks, seeing a larger context. Dual-process view: insight likely uses both analytic and intuitive processes, intuition more influential (Lin et al. 2011).
numbers: Cited facts: Segal 2004 a 4-min break helped insight as much as a 12-min break; Wagner et al. 2004 sleep after training gave about twice the insight solutions; Ovington et al. 2015 almost 20% of Australian respondents reported never having an insight; Kounios and Beeman 2009 EEG alpha and gamma activity about 300 ms before insight solutions.
limits: Secondary encyclopedia source. The page does not name Wallas, Ohlsson or Knoblich. Numbers are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Four stages map onto the schema: attempts (S0-S5), impasse (S6), reframe (O6), verification (S8).

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider and Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Test of Representational Change Theory with matchstick arithmetic (Roman numerals). Problems needing a constraint of wider scope relaxed (value, then operator, then tautology) are harder. Problems needing a tight chunk decomposed are harder than loose-chunk ones. Impasse arises from the initial representation and is broken by relaxing constraints or decomposing chunks.
numbers: Exp 1A: N=20 undergraduates, 5-min limit, two blocks. Difficulty order C<B<A and D<A: F(3,57)=7.11, p<.001. Block effect F(1,19)=14.41, p<.01 (more solved in block 2). Type D solved 75% in block 1 vs 90% in block 2. Exp 1B: 38 participants, same order. Exp 2: N=78; 66% solved in block 1, 96% in block 2.
limits: One task family (matchstick arithmetic), small samples, time-limited. Later work found the Aha-correctness link weak for matchstick tasks (see a12).
agent_relevance: Gives an ordering for O6: try cheap constraint relaxations first (values), then operators, then the goal form; decompose tight chunks last.

source: Knoblich et al. (1999), transfer and similarity results
finding: Transfer from block 1 to block 2 was larger for problem types that were harder in block 1 (B and C), and absent for type A. This fits learned constraint relaxation, not surface similarity of the problems.
numbers: Type x block interaction F(3,57)=3.24, p<.05. Transfer: B p<.05, C p<.001, A p=.80, D p=.13 (not significant). Exp 2 (N=78) similarity conditions, block-2 solution 95-99%, no similarity effect (means 82, 82, 80, 83%).
limits: Small N in Exp 1; one domain.
agent_relevance: Once a reframing move works, keep it as a reusable move for later items in the same session.

source: Sio and Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
finding: Positive incubation effect overall. Divergent-thinking tasks gain more than linguistic or visual insight tasks. Longer preparation gives a bigger effect. A high-demand task during the break shrinks the effect. A low-demand task beat rest for linguistic insight problems.
numbers: 117 studies, 3,606 participants, median n=25 per study; 85 positive effects. Unweighted mean unbiased effect 0.41 (SD 0.71, CI 0.28-0.54); outlier-capped mean 0.36 (SD 0.51, CI 0.26-0.45). Random-effects weighted mean 0.29 (SD 0.04, CI 0.21-0.39). Cochran Q=173.99, df=113, p<.001; between-study variance .0834. Median 0.26.
limits: Small effects and large heterogeneity. Mostly Western undergraduates with small samples. Authors found no clear publication bias from the funnel plot.
agent_relevance: Supports a cheap set-aside-and-return step only on a signal (G1). The effect is small, so test it at equal tokens (G7).

source: Sio and Ormerod (2009), misleading-cue moderator
finding: For linguistic problems, incubation helped more when the problem carried misleading cues (fixation). This supports the forgetting-of-fixation account. For visual problems the pattern was not the same.
numbers: 29 studies on misleading cues (25 linguistic). Weighted effect: linguistic with misleading cue M=0.36 (SD 0.09) vs without M=0.17 (SD 0.06); visual with misleading cue M=0.18 (SD 0.39) vs without M=0.26 (SD 0.08). Meta-regressions explain about R2=.20-.21.
limits: Only four visual studies in the cue set; very wide SD for visual.
agent_relevance: A break helps when the first framing was misleading: a fresh sample or restated problem after failure fits this boundary.

source: Sio and Ormerod (2009), theoretical conclusion
finding: Authors conclude that both the unconscious-work account and the conscious-restructuring account get support, but each only for particular problem types. Divergent tasks look knowledge-based; insight tasks look strategic.
numbers: Pooled numbers in a04. Appendix lists 117 studies with break lengths from 0.25 min to 1,440 min.
quote: evidence for each appears to be specific to particular problem types
limits: The authors say too few studies fit to draw strong cross-study conclusions.
agent_relevance: There is no single 'incubation' mechanism, so do not build one operator for all task types.

source: Sio and Ormerod (2009), Wallas stage model and rival accounts
finding: Wallas (1926) proposed incubation as the second of four phases (preparation, incubation, illumination, verification). Three accounts of incubation are weighed: unconscious work (spreading activation), conscious work during the break, and forgetting of fixation or opportunistic assimilation. Insight is characterised as sudden, unpredictable, nonverbalizable solution discovery.
numbers: Authors count 5,510 Google Scholar articles (1997-2007) on incubation with creativity, insight or problem, plus 1,970 more. Earlier narrative reviews had only about 10 studies.
limits: Intro framing only.
agent_relevance: Verification as a separate stage matches S8. For an LLM, 'incubation' can only mean a context reset or restated problem, not hidden compute.

source: Jung-Beeman, Bowden, Haberman et al. (2004) Neural activity when people solve verbal problems with insight
finding: Compound remote associate problems with self-report of insight. fMRI: right anterior superior temporal gyrus more active for insight than non-insight solutions. EEG: a burst of gamma activity in the same area beginning 0.3 s before insight solutions. Read as a sudden shift to distant semantic links.
numbers: Exp 1 (13 subjects): 59% of problems solved; insight reported for 56% (SD 18.2) of solutions, no insight 41% (SD 18.9), other 2%. RH aSTG peak signal difference 0.25% (0.30% at one TR); 12 of 13 subjects showed more signal for insight (0.03-0.35%).
quote: Neural correlates of insight vs non-insight
limits: Small samples. Self-report defines the condition. Verbal CRA problems only.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that the solution arrives as a discrete jump, not gradual progress; no clean mapping to token-level compute.

source: Jung-Beeman et al. (2004), background on warmth and discrete transitions
finding: Reviews that on insight problems solvers report little or no progress until shortly before solving (Metcalfe 1986; Metcalfe and Wiebe 1987), while non-insight problems show gradually rising closeness. Anagram speed-accuracy data show a discrete jump from no information to full accuracy (Kounios and Smith 1995).
numbers: No new numbers; cites the warmth-rating studies.
quote: little or no progress until shortly before they actually solve the problem
limits: Second-hand description. Weisberg and Alba (1981) and Perkins (2000) argue insight and non-insight differ only in emotion, not mechanism.
agent_relevance: Flat progress followed by a jump is a possible impasse signature; a code-side progress meter could flag flat progress before a switch.

source: Webb, Little and Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem: investigating insight in problem solving across task types
finding: Aha reports predict accuracy for classic insight problems and compound remote associates, but only weakly for non-insight problems. Both classic insight and non-insight problems can be solved with insight and with analysis. Self-report is needed because task type does not define the process.
numbers: Exp 1: 193 students recruited (9 removed); Exp 1a: 82 (8 removed); Exp 2: 129 (12 removed). Accuracy-Aha r for classic insight .50/.40/.495, CRA .41/.40/.39, non-insight .02/.24/.19 (Exp 1/1a/2). Accuracy classic insight .51/.49/.45, non-insight .54/.64/.56, CRA .37/.45/.47. Multilevel logit: impasse -1.08, pleasure +1.11, surprise -0.19.
limits: Student samples. One cell (Exp 1a non-insight Aha mean 64.40) looked inconsistent with the text in extraction. Self-report cannot separate a special process from a feeling.
agent_relevance: Do not pick restructuring by task label; use a measured impasse signal (G1).

source: Danek and Wiley (2017) What about false insights? Deconstructing the Aha! experience along its multiple dimensions
finding: False insights exist: Aha experiences accompany wrong solutions. Aha has components Pleasure, Suddenness and Certainty. Correct solutions came faster with stronger Aha, Pleasure, Suddenness and Certainty. Incorrect solutions carried more Surprise; correct ones more Relief.
numbers: 70 participants, 35 magic-trick videos, 2,450 observations; 603 timeouts and 69 missing dropped; of 1,778 solutions 36.8% (654) correct and 63.2% (1,124) incorrect.
limits: Magic tricks only, free-text solutions, self-report.
agent_relevance: A felt 'aha' (or a model writing 'wait, actually') is not verification; S8 must test the new answer on something held out (G3).

source: Wiley and Miller (2026) Aha! ratings as metacognitive judgments
finding: Aha ratings behave like judgments inferred from cues, not a direct readout of restructuring. Aha was highest for correct solutions that began with a correct first move, not for solutions after an incorrect first move that needed representational change. Aha tracks correctness more than restructuring.
numbers: 377 introductory psychology students; spatial object-move puzzles with a 3-min limit. Aha-correctness effect F(1,1091)=112.17, p<.001; strong for the Fish and Triangle puzzles, weaker for matchstick puzzles.
limits: One lab, spatial puzzles, US students. Matchstick results are mixed across studies (Kizilirmak 2021 yes, Strickland 2022 no).
agent_relevance: Do not use the model's own confidence or 'aha' wording as the trigger or the proof of a reframe (G2, G5).

source: Kim (2026) Illumination onset: a theoretical neuroscience framework for the sudden Aha moment
finding: Theoretical framework for the illumination stage of the Wallas model, proposing mechanisms for the sudden onset of the Aha moment (Behavioral Sciences 16(10):1740). It is a theory paper.
numbers: No empirical numbers extracted.
limits: Only the opening and framing were read; theory-level claims, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Background for the illumination state; adds no new operator.

source: Becker, Sommer, Cabeza et al. (2025) Insight predicts subsequent memory via cortical representational change and hippocampal activity (Nature Communications 16:4341)
finding: fMRI with Mooney images: insight (sudden object recognition) shows stronger representational change in visual cortex, with amygdala and hippocampus activation. Representational change and hippocampal effects predict later memory of the solution.
numbers: N=31 analysed. Insight ratings (1-4): positive emotion M=2.8 (SD .41), suddenness M=3.0 (SD .39), certainty M=3.16 (SD .34); loadings on one latent factor .53-.65.
limits: Visual perceptual rechunking, not verbal or logical insight. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Insight solutions are remembered better: store a reframe that passed S8 as a durable lesson.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI delivers creative output but struggles with thinking processes
finding: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4 and GPT-4o beat humans on divergent thinking, convergent thinking (RAT) and several insight tasks, but lost on creative writing. On a representational-change task, models were far less accurate than humans. Models mostly used reasoning; humans used transformation strategies.
numbers: Chinese character puzzle: humans below GPT-4o (estimate -0.21, CI -0.28 to -0.14), above GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (+0.09). Stumpers: humans above GPT-3.5 (+0.20) and GPT-4 (+0.06), below GPT-4o (-0.06). Rebus: humans below GPT-4-turbo (-0.32) and GPT-4o (-0.39). Representational-change task (24 problems): humans higher than GPT-4-turbo by 0.46 (CI .41-.51) and GPT-4o by 0.31 (CI .25-.36).
limits: Chinese-language tasks, preprint, classic puzzles may be in training data. High insight accuracy may be retrieval.
agent_relevance: High accuracy on named insight puzzles is weak evidence of restructuring; use fresh, renewable items (G8).

source: Zhang et al. (2025), Study 2 association results
finding: AI produced lower forward flow than humans in free and chain association. On the RAT, AI wrong answers were closer in meaning to the stimulus. Authors read this as local semantic search near the input, with no remote association, and no human-like novelty-appropriateness trade-off.
numbers: Exp 5: 61 human participants, 61 instances per GPT model.
limits: Preprint; forward flow measured with embeddings; Chinese-language setting.
agent_relevance: Distant-link search may need to be forced by code (sample far from the first framing) rather than asked of the model.

source: Orru, Piarulli, Conversano and Gemignani (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT
finding: ChatGPT solved verbal insight problems about as well as the most probable outcome for human participants on both sets, and was within the top 5% of probable human outcomes on practice problems and the pooled set.
numbers: 30 problems (practice and transfer sets, max score 15 each); human solution rates from 20 subjects per problem.
limits: Only the abstract and summary were read in full. Classic problems may be in training data; early ChatGPT version.
agent_relevance: Early parity claim; later fresh-item benchmarks show a large gap (a18, a19).

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: lateral thinking puzzles for large language models
finding: Multiple-choice lateral-thinking puzzles (sentence and word) with semantic and context reconstructions to test memorisation. ChatGPT was far from human; errors came from memorisation and misleading commonsense associations.
numbers: About 1.1K items. ChatGPT 53% and 63% on the two subtasks vs random 25% and human 92%; about a third of models at or below random. Open-ended human vs ChatGPT quality 2.64 vs 2.62 of 5; humans gave up on 18% of items.
limits: Multiple-choice format lowers difficulty. One 2023 ChatGPT version; the NazoNazo paper notes GPT-4 later exceeded 98% on it, so it saturated.
agent_relevance: The commonsense lure is LLM fixation; a code check on reconstructed variants catches memorised answers (G3).

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025, v2 2026) The metacognitive bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal fundamental limits of machine insight
finding: NazoNazo benchmark of 201 Japanese riddles, with a 120-item human-comparison subset. Frontier models were far below humans except GPT-5, inside the human CI. Main failure: verification failure, where the model writes the correct candidate in its thought log but does not endorse it.
numbers: Humans n=126, mean 52.9% (CI 46.6-59.2). 38 LLMs zero-shot: non-reasoning mean 7.6%, reasoning mean 17.6%. Verification failures = 5.23% to 39.34% of wrong answers: Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview 5.23% (9 VF, 29 correct), DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.57% (48 VF, 42 correct), Claude Opus 4 25.00% (35 VF, 61 correct), Grok 4 39.34% (48 VF, 72 correct).
limits: Japanese wordplay may not generalise. Thought logs are not faithful traces. GPT-5 result is observational, CI overlap is not equivalence.
agent_relevance: Directly supports S8: the missing step is endorsing a candidate that was already generated. Code can compare mid-trace candidates with the final answer and test them.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025/2026), few-shot and recognition result
finding: Models recognised the items as riddles without instruction, yet recognition alone did not give good performance. Reasoning-inclusive few-shot demos improved accuracy in all four models tested and significantly in two; the top model did not reach significance.
numbers: Supplementary study with four models; base rates in a19.
limits: Gains not uniform and not shown across multiple demo sets.
agent_relevance: Search and verify strategy can be primed, but test any demo at equal tokens (G7).

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The illusion of insight in reasoning models
finding: Mid-trace shifts ('Wait...') in RL-trained reasoners are rare, do not grow with training, and seldom help accuracy. Shifts mark unstable inference. Spontaneous shifts do not help even at high entropy, but an externally triggered reconsideration helps, most at high entropy.
numbers: 1M+ traces; GRPO runs on Qwen2.5 and Llama; Math (MATH-500), cryptic crosswords, Rush Hour. Shifts in 6.31% of traces. Math raw accuracy gap with a shift: -7.40 pp at high entropy, -22.88 pp at low entropy. Forced reconsideration: Math 0.3221 to 0.4062 (+8.41 pp; 50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong over 320,000 paired samples); crosswords +0.45 pp (5,380 vs 5,004); Rush Hour +0.01 pp.
limits: Shift detection uses a GPT-4o judge and lexical cues; small models; gains concentrated in math.
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of G1: self-triggered reframing is noise; a code-triggered reconsideration on a high-uncertainty signal helps. Matches S6 impasse detector then O6.

source: Guo et al. (2025) DeepSeek-R1: incentivizing reasoning capability in LLMs via reinforcement learning (the 'aha moment')
finding: Reports an 'aha moment' in an intermediate DeepSeek-R1-Zero: a sudden rise in the word 'wait' during reflection, with the model re-evaluating its approach. Framed as RL self-evolution.
numbers: AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 77.9% during RL; thinking length grew steadily. The 'wait' jump is in the supplement (Fig 9b).
limits: Anecdotal; the paper itself cites Liu et al. 2025 'There may not be aha moment in R1-Zero-like training'. a21 finds such shifts rare and seldom helpful.
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'wait' tokens as insight; keep restructuring a code-triggered operator.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a mental set?
finding: Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B and GPT-4o on mathematical-equivalence problems with mental-set conditions adapted from DeCaro (2016). Few-shot plus zero-shot CoT raised exact match for all models; plain few-shot did poorly. Examples did not cut the number of steps. Under CoT, 70B and GPT-4o did better on complex than shortcut problems.
numbers: Metrics exact match and step count; three models; FS vs FS+CoT; no human data.
limits: Short paper, three models, one task. Reading CoT as a 'mental set shift' is interpretation.
agent_relevance: Reasoning prompts add steps and can hide a shortcut; test shortcut-hunting as an explicit operator.

source: Gestalt account of impasse and restructuring as stated in Wiley and Miller (2026)
finding: Gestalt view (Duncker, Katona, Kohler, Maier, Wertheimer): insight is restructuring, a sudden shift of problem representation from an unproductive to a productive approach. Impasse (feeling stuck) is thought to push the solver to explore other representations. The impasse-then-insight sequence is theory, tested only indirectly.
numbers: No numbers; background section.
limits: Cue-based Aha work (a12) questions whether Aha reflects restructuring.
agent_relevance: Supports the S6 then O6 order; open question is whether the model needs an explicit impasse signal.

source: Ohlsson (1992) Information-processing explanations of insight and related phenomena (Representational Change Theory)
finding: Not opened directly. As summarised in the opened Knoblich 1999, Zhang 2025 and Danek and Wiley 2017 papers: the initial representation is incomplete or wrong, search fails (impasse), then constraint relaxation, chunk decomposition or re-encoding changes the representation. Ohlsson (1984b) also theorised 'erroneous insights'.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand. Rival: progress monitoring theory (MacGregor et al. 2001), not opened.
agent_relevance: Core design reference for O6 (reframe by relaxing a named constraint).

source: Vallee-Tourangeau et al. (2020) Incubation and interactivity in insight problem solving
finding: Cheap necklace problem: more physical interactivity (metal chains vs pen and paper) improved performance at Time 1. A 2-week gap gave an incubation gain, larger with high interactivity. When the format changed after the gap, only people with high interactivity at Time 2 improved.
numbers: Two experiments; participant counts not extracted; significant improvement after a 2-week gap (Psychological Research 84(1):128-139).
limits: Counts not read; one problem; distributed-cognition framing rivals pure restructuring.
agent_relevance: Acting on external material (running code, drawing) may beat re-thinking; favours operators that execute.

source: Wiley and Miller (2026), first-move analysis
finding: Split by first move, the Aha-correctness effect came from solutions that followed a correct first move, not from those that followed an incorrect first move. If incorrect-first-move solutions are the restructuring ones, restructuring did not drive Aha.
numbers: Same dataset as a12 (N=377).
limits: Aha-accuracy effects are solid for verbal and magic-trick tasks but mixed for matchsticks.
agent_relevance: Cheap check: log the first attempt; reframes after a wrong first attempt are the true O6 cases to count.
